items.prompt: What is the one defining constraint of refactoring, as opposed to rewriting?
choices: The code must end up shorter than it started
Observable behavior must stay exactly the same, before and after
It must use fewer functions than the original
It must be done in a single commit
items.explanation: Refactoring's whole claim is that the same inputs produce the same outputs before and after — how the internals are organized is what changes, not what the program does from the outside. Length, function count, and commit count are all incidental to that.
items.reference:
🔄 Refactoring — same inputs, same outputs, before and after
🛠️ Rewriting — behavior is expected/allowed to change
🧪 The test suite is what tells you which one actually happened
items.learnMore:
RefactoringRewriting
Same observable behaviorBehavior may change, often on purpose
Tiny, individually-verifiable stepsUsually one large change
Existing tests are the safety netNew tests have to be written from scratch

If you can't say "behavior didn't change, provably," it isn't a refactor — even if the resulting code looks cleaner.

items.prompt: Dana reorganizes calculateOrderTotal into five smaller functions, and along the way also changes the free-shipping threshold from $75 to $50. Is this a refactor?
choices: Yes — the internal structure is what changed, that's the definition
No — changing the shipping threshold changes observable behavior, so this is a rewrite wearing a refactor's name
Yes, as long as all the tests still pass
It depends on how many functions were extracted
items.explanation: Splitting into five functions is structural and fine. But changing $75 to $50 changes what the function returns for orders between $50 and $75 — that's a real behavior change bundled into what's being called a refactor, which defeats the point of the label.

items.prompt: Why does the distinction between refactoring and rewriting matter in practice?
choices: It doesn't — they're just two words for the same activity
Rewriting is always the safer choice
They call for very different amounts of caution and different safety nets
Refactoring is only a term used for legacy COBOL systems
items.explanation: A refactor can lean on existing, already-trusted tests and tiny reversible steps. A rewrite can't make that claim — it needs new verification built from scratch. Treating a rewrite as if it were a refactor (or vice versa) means applying the wrong amount of caution.

items.prompt: A tangled function has zero automated tests. What's the first move in a safe refactor of it?
choices: Start extracting functions immediately — tests can be added afterward
Write tests that pin down the function's current behavior, before touching its structure
Rewrite the function from scratch, since there's nothing to preserve
Skip testing entirely if the function is small enough to review by eye
items.explanation: Without tests, there's no way to verify a structural change didn't alter behavior — that verification is refactoring's entire justification for being 'safe.' Characterization tests, written first, are what make every later step checkable instead of just hopeful.
items.reference:
🧪 No tests → "behavior didn't change" is just an opinion
📌 Characterization tests — written to pin down current behavior, quirks included
✅ Safety net exists → small steps become checkable, not just hopeful
items.learnMore: A refactor's entire claim is "the observable behavior is unchanged." Without an automated test suite already covering that behavior, there's no way to check that claim other than by inspection — which is exactly the kind of manual verification that misses regressions in tangled code. Characterization tests record what the code currently does, including any quirks, so that every later structural step has something concrete to be checked against. Writing them isn't optional preparation — it's the first step of the discipline itself.

items.prompt: Why is 'refactoring without tests' considered riskier than ordinary refactoring, rather than just 'extra careful' refactoring?
choices: Because it takes longer without tests
Because without a safety net, there's no way to verify the core claim that behavior didn't change — it becomes an unverified rewrite in disguise
Because most languages require a test framework to run at all
It isn't riskier — careful manual review is just as reliable
items.explanation: Refactoring's safety comes specifically from being able to check the 'behavior unchanged' claim mechanically. Remove that check and the activity is functionally an unverified rewrite, no matter how careful or slow you go by hand.

A test written to record what the code currently does, quirks included, so later changes can be checked against it
A performance benchmark run before a refactor
A test that only runs in a staging environment
items.explanation: A characterization test isn't about what's 'correct' — it's a snapshot of actual current behavior, including any quirks or bugs, so that a later refactor has something honest to verify itself against.

items.prompt: What is a "code smell"?
choices: A syntax error the compiler catches
A surface signal that a design problem probably lives underneath — a prompt to look closer, not proof
A style-guide violation flagged by a linter
A synonym for a bug that's already been reported
items.explanation: A smell isn't a verdict — it's a signal worth investigating. Some smells in small doses are harmless; the judgment call is deciding when a smell is actually costing something worth fixing.
items.reference:
👃 A code smell is a surface signal, not proof of a problem
👀 It is a prompt to look closer — not an automatic rewrite order
⚖️ Small doses of a smell can be fine; judgment decides when it is worth acting on
items.learnMore:

Duplicated logicSame check written more than onceFix one copy, the other keeps old behavior
Long functionMany unrelated things, one blockHard to hold the whole thing in mind to change one part
Deep nestingif inside if inside ifEach branch multiplies the paths to reason about

items.prompt: Boxtree's function checks 'is this a real member' in three places. Two check `isMember && !membershipSuspended`; the third checks only `isMember`. What does this concretely illustrate?
choices: That duplication is always harmless as long as the logic is short
That duplicated logic can silently drift out of sync with itself, and nobody can tell by reading whether that's a bug or intentional
That the third check is definitely correct and the other two are wrong
That JavaScript doesn't support shared functions
items.explanation: This is exactly the risk duplicated logic creates: three copies of 'the same idea,' one of which has already diverged, with no way to tell from the code alone whether that divergence was intentional or a mistake.
items.reference:
⚠️ Boxtree's gift-wrap branch checks only isMember — the other two also check !membershipSuspended
🐛 That mismatch is a real, currently-live latent bug hiding in the duplication
items.learnMore: Duplicated logic isn't just extra typing — every copy is a separate place a future edit has to remember to update. Boxtree's three membership checks already show the failure mode: two copies check both isMember and !membershipSuspended, the third checks only isMember. Whether that third copy was a typo or a deliberate choice, nobody can tell just by reading it — which is exactly the ambiguity a single shared function would have prevented.

items.prompt: What's the general risk duplicated logic creates, beyond extra lines of code?
choices: It makes the file larger, which slows down compilation
A bug fix or behavior change applied to one copy can silently fail to reach the others
It always causes a runtime error
It prevents the code from being minified
items.explanation: The core danger of duplication is that a fix applied to one copy doesn't automatically apply to the others — leaving them to quietly diverge, which is exactly what happened to Boxtree's third membership check.

items.prompt: Which of these is a legitimate reason to skip refactoring a tangled function, even though it has real smells?
choices: The function is scheduled to be deleted and replaced next sprint
The function was written by someone who left the company
The function has more than 3 code smells
The function doesn't use TypeScript
items.explanation: Effort spent cleaning up code with no future doesn't pay itself back. The other options aren't good reasons on their own — who wrote it and how many smells it has don't determine whether refactoring now is worth the time.
items.reference:
🗑️ Code scheduled for deletion — no future to pay the cleanup back
⏱️ Hard deadline, no slack for a false start
🚫 No tests, no time to write them first
items.learnMore: Small-step refactoring still costs real time and attention. It's worth skipping when the code has no future to pay that investment back (it's about to be deleted), when there's no room to safely revert a bad step (a hard deadline with zero slack), or when the safety net itself isn't there and there's no time to build it. In any of these, a smaller, more surgical change — even a slightly uglier one — can be the more honest choice than starting work you might not finish safely.

items.prompt: Under a hard deadline with no slack for a false start, what's the more honest choice than starting the full small-step refactor loop?
choices: Skip tests entirely to save time
A smaller, more surgical (even slightly uglier) change, with the full refactor scheduled separately when there's room to do it safely
Refactor everything at once in a single large commit to save round-trips
Refactor as normal — deadlines don't change the safe approach
items.explanation: The refactor loop's safety depends on being able to revert a bad step and try again. Without slack for that, a smaller surgical patch — while less elegant — is more honest than starting a multi-step refactor that might get abandoned halfway.

items.prompt: In the safe-refactor loop, what happens immediately after making one small structural change?
choices: Move on to the next smell — testing happens at the very end
Run the full test suite before doing anything else
Write documentation for the change
Ask a teammate to review it before running any tests
items.explanation: The loop is: make one small change, then immediately run the full test suite, then commit if green or revert if red. Testing after every single step (not just at the end) is what keeps each step independently verifiable.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Pick the smallest change addressing one smell
2️⃣ Make that one change
3️⃣ Run the full test suite
✅ Green → commit. 🔁 Red → revert and retry
items.learnMore: The safe-refactor loop is: pick the smallest structural change that addresses one smell, make it, run the full test suite, then either commit (if green) or revert (if red) before picking the next change. Each pass through the loop is independently verified — that's what makes a red result at step 3 of six tell you exactly which step broke something, instead of leaving you searching through a whole session's worth of changes.

items.prompt: If the test suite goes red right after a refactoring step, what's the loop's prescribed response?
choices: Keep the change and immediately start debugging the failing test in place
Revert that one step, then pick the next attempt from the last known-green state
Disable the failing test and continue to the next step
Push the change anyway and fix it in a follow-up commit
items.explanation: A red result means this specific step didn't preserve behavior. Reverting it costs minutes, not a whole session, and keeps every commit that lands trustworthy — which is the entire point of doing this in small steps.

items.prompt: Why does the loop commit after each individual step, rather than batching several steps into one commit at the end?

So that if something later turns out to be wrong, the search space for 'which change caused it' is as small as possible
Because CI systems require one commit per file changed
It doesn't matter — committing once at the end is equally safe
items.explanation: Small, individually-verified commits mean a later problem points at exactly one step, not a search through several bundled changes. That's the entire value proposition of the loop, not just a stylistic preference.

items.prompt: Dana could rewrite all of calculateOrderTotal in one sitting and run the tests once at the end, instead of six separate verified steps. What's the concrete downside of the one-shot approach?
choices: It takes strictly more total time than doing six small steps
If a test fails, there's no way to tell which of the many changed lines caused it
It's not possible to run tests after a large rewrite
There is no downside — both approaches are equally safe
items.explanation: A single test run at the end of a large rewrite can tell you something broke, but not what or where. Smaller, individually-tested steps narrow that search to just the most recent step.
items.reference:
🔍 One big rewrite, one test run at the end → a failure could be anywhere in 68 lines
🧩 Six small steps, tested after each → a failure points at exactly one step
items.learnMore: Smaller steps don't reduce the total amount of change eventually made — they reduce how much of it has to be re-verified together if something breaks. A step that fails its test run reverts cheaply, in minutes; a whole rewrite that fails at the end has to be searched, line by line, to find which part of a much larger diff is actually at fault.

items.prompt: What does reverting cost when a refactor is done in small, individually-committed steps, compared to one large rewrite?
choices: The same either way — reverting is always trivial
Minutes — just the most recent step, instead of a whole session's uncommitted work
Reverting is impossible once a step is committed
More, because there are more commits to undo
items.explanation: Because each step is committed only after its own test run passes, reverting a bad step means throwing away just that one step — not the whole rewrite that came before it.

items.prompt: A pull request both restructures calculateOrderTotal and adds the loyalty discount, all in one diff. A test fails. What's the actual problem this creates?
choices: Nothing — as long as the final tests pass, the commit history doesn't matter
There's no way to tell whether the restructuring broke something or the new discount logic is wrong
The PR will be too large for GitHub to display
It only matters for open-source projects with external reviewers
items.explanation: A refactor commit is normally checked against 'did behavior stay the same,' a feature commit against 'is the new behavior correct.' Bundling both into one commit means a failure can't cleanly answer either question.
items.reference:
🧪 Refactor commit → checked against "did behavior stay the same"
✨ Feature commit → checked against "is the new behavior correct"
⛔ One commit doing both answers neither question cleanly
items.learnMore: A refactor commit's entire evidence of safety is "the existing tests, unchanged, still pass." A feature commit's evidence of correctness is "new tests, written for the new behavior, now also pass." Mixing the two into one commit means a failing test can no longer tell you which question it's answering — was the restructuring unsafe, or is the new logic wrong? Keeping them separate keeps both questions independently checkable.

items.prompt: Why can't 'the tests are green' be trusted as evidence a refactor was safe, if that same commit also introduces new behavior?
choices: Because green tests are never trustworthy
Because the tests are now also covering the new behavior, so passing doesn't isolate whether the old behavior was actually preserved
Because CI systems randomly report false positives
It can still be trusted — new behavior doesn't affect old test results
items.explanation: If new tests for new behavior are added in the same commit as a structural change, a green run no longer proves the structural change alone was behavior-preserving — the two are now entangled in the same verification.
items.reference:

✨ Feature commit → checked against "is the new behavior correct"
⛔ One commit doing both answers neither question cleanly

items.prompt: Boxtree's function checked `customer.isMember && !customer.membershipSuspended` in two different places. Implement `isActiveMember(customer)` so both sites can call one shared function instead of repeating the condition.
items.explanation: This reproduces exactly what the two original call sites computed inline — a member counts as active only when both isMember is true and membershipSuspended is falsy. Extracting it means both sites now share one definition of 'active member' instead of two copies that could quietly drift apart.
items.reference:

It also makes the current rule easy to read and test in isolation, instead of being inferred by comparing several near-identical if-conditions scattered through a larger function.

items.prompt: Replace this region-branching tax logic with a lookup table. `calculateTax(taxableAmount, region)`: US is 7%, CA is 5%, EU is 20%, any other region is 0%.
items.explanation: `TAX_RATES[region] ?? 0` reproduces the original if/else chain's final `else { taxRate = 0; }` for any region not in the map — the `??` operator only falls back when the lookup is `undefined` or `null`, which is exactly what an unlisted key produces.
items.reference:
📋 if/else chain branching on region → one object keyed by region
0️⃣ ?? 0 reproduces the old else-branch fallback exactly
items.learnMore: An if/else chain that branches repeatedly on the same value — here, region — is a direct match for Replace Conditional with Lookup Table. The nullish-coalescing fallback (`?? 0`) is what makes the replacement behavior-preserving: any region not explicitly listed in the map falls through to the same default the old chain's final `else` produced, rather than silently returning `undefined`.
